ELECTRICITY BASICS: STUDY NOTES
CONCEPT 1 OF 5
Electric current
Key idea
Electric current is the flow of electric charge through a conductor. In a metal
wire the moving charges are electrons. The bigger the current, the more
charge passes a point in the wire every second.
Facts to know
1. Current is the rate of flow of charge. It is the amount of charge that
passes a point in a circuit each second.
2. The formula is I = Q / t, where I is the current in amperes (A), Q is the
charge in coulombs (C) and t is the time in seconds (s). It can be
rearranged as Q = I × t.
3. A current of one ampere means that one coulomb of charge passes a
point every second. A current of 2 A means that 2 coulombs pass a point
every second.
4. Current is measured with an ammeter. An ammeter must be connected in
series with the component, so that all of the current flows through it.
5. Current flows only in a complete circuit. A break anywhere in the loop
stops the current in the whole loop.
6. By convention, current is drawn flowing from the positive terminal of a
cell, round the circuit, to the negative terminal. The electrons move the
opposite way, from the negative terminal to the positive terminal.
Worked examples
Example 1. A charge of 12 C passes a point in a wire in 4 s. I = Q / t = 12 /
4 = 3 A. The current is 3 A.
Example 2. How much charge passes a point in 10 s when the current is
0.5 A? Q = I × t = 0.5 × 10 = 5 C.

CONCEPT 2 OF 5
Potential difference (voltage)
Key idea
Recall from Concept 1 that current is a flow of charge. Charge flows round a
circuit only if something pushes it. The push comes from a cell or battery,
which gives energy to the charge. The energy given to each coulomb of
charge is called the potential difference, or voltage.
Facts to know
1. Potential difference (voltage) between two points is the energy
transferred to or from each coulomb of charge as it moves between those
points.
2. The formula is V = W / Q, where V is the potential difference in volts (V),
W is the energy in joules (J) and Q is the charge in coulombs (C). It can be
rearranged as W = V × Q.
3. A potential difference of one volt means one joule of energy for each
coulomb of charge. A 9 V battery gives 9 J to every coulomb that passes
through it.
4. A cell transfers energy to the charge. A component such as a bulb
transfers energy from the charge to its surroundings as heat and light.
5. Potential difference is measured with a voltmeter. A voltmeter must be
connected in parallel, across the component being measured.
6. Potential difference is always measured between two points. It does not
flow through a wire. The charge flows, and the potential difference is the
push that makes it flow.
Worked examples
Example 1. A 9 V battery moves 2 C of charge through a circuit. W = V × Q
= 9 × 2 = 18 J. The battery transfers 18 J of energy.
Example 2. A bulb transfers 30 J of energy while 5 C of charge passes
through it. V = W / Q = 30 / 5 = 6 V. The potential difference across the bulb
is 6 V.

CONCEPT 3 OF 5
Resistance
Key idea
Recall from Concept 1 that current is a flow of charge. As the charges move
through a material they collide with its atoms, so the material opposes the
flow. This opposition to the flow of current is called resistance.
Facts to know
1. Resistance is the opposition of a component or wire to the flow of electric
current.
2. Resistance is measured in ohms (symbol Ω).
3. A longer wire has a greater resistance than a shorter wire of the same
material and thickness. If the length is doubled, the resistance is doubled.
4. A thicker wire has a smaller resistance than a thinner wire of the same
material and length. If the cross-sectional area is doubled, the resistance
is halved.
5. Different materials have different resistances. Copper has a low
resistance, so it is used for connecting wires. Nichrome has a high
resistance, so it is used in heating elements.
6. The resistance of a metal wire rises when the wire gets hotter, because
the atoms vibrate more and collide with more of the moving charge.
7. For a metal wire at constant temperature, the resistance stays the same
whatever the potential difference across it or the current through it.
Worked examples
Example 1. A wire has a resistance of 6 Ω. A second wire is made of the
same material and has the same thickness, but it is three times as long. Its
resistance is 3 × 6 = 18 Ω.
Example 2. A third wire has the same material and length as the first wire,
but twice the cross-sectional area. Its resistance is 6 / 2 = 3 Ω.

CONCEPT 4 OF 5
Ohm’s law
Key idea
Concept 2 and Concept 3 meet here. The potential difference (Concept 2)
pushes the current round the circuit, and the resistance (Concept 3) limits
how big the current can be. Ohm’s law links the three quantities.
Facts to know
1. Ohm’s law states that V = I × R, where V is the potential difference in
volts, I is the current in amperes and R is the resistance in ohms.
2. The law can be rearranged as I = V / R and as R = V / I.
3. When the resistance stays constant, doubling the potential difference
doubles the current.
4. When the potential difference stays constant, doubling the resistance
halves the current.
5. A graph of current against potential difference for a metal wire at
constant temperature is a straight line through the origin.
6. The graph for a filament bulb is a curve, because the filament gets hot
and its resistance rises as the current increases.
7. To find any one of V, I or R, you must know the other two.
Worked examples
Example 1. A 12 V supply is connected across a 6 Ω resistor. I = V / R = 12
/ 6 = 2 A.
Example 2. A current of 0.5 A flows through a resistor when the potential
difference across it is 8 V. R = V / I = 8 / 0.5 = 16 Ω.

CONCEPT 5 OF 5
Series circuits
Key idea
Ohm’s law (Concept 4) can be used to analyse a series circuit. In a series
circuit the components are connected one after another, so there is only one
path for the charge to follow.
Facts to know
1. In a series circuit there is only one path for the charge.
2. The current is the same at every point in a series circuit, because the
charge has no other path to take and cannot pile up or disappear along
the way.
3. An ammeter placed before, between or after the components of a series
circuit shows the same reading.
4. The potential differences across the components add up to the potential
difference of the supply: V total = V1 + V2 + V3.
5. The total resistance of components in series is the sum of their
resistances: R total = R1 + R2 + R3.
6. Adding another resistor in series increases the total resistance, so the
current in the circuit gets smaller.
7. Two identical bulbs in series with a cell share the potential difference of
the cell equally. If the resistances are different, the component with the
larger resistance gets the larger share of the potential difference.
Worked example
Example. A 12 V cell is connected in series with a 4 Ω resistor and an 8 Ω
resistor. R total = 4 + 8 = 12 Ω. I = V / R = 12 / 12 = 1 A. The same 1 A
flows through both resistors. Across the 4 Ω resistor: V = I × R = 1 × 4 = 4
V. Across the 8 Ω resistor: V = 1 × 8 = 8 V. Check: 4 V + 8 V = 12 V, which
equals the potential difference of the cell.
